Chapter 31: Google Cloud Organization, Folders, Projects and
Landing Zones
Designing a resource hierarchy and foundation blueprint
Why this chapter matters: Google Cloud hierarchy determines inherited IAM, organization
policies, billing and workload isolation. A durable design uses projects as strong lifecycle
boundaries and centralizes foundation capabilities. Learning Objectives

Explain the architecture, responsibility boundaries and major trade-offs of organization, folders and project
hierarchy.

Design landing-zone design and enterprise foundation blueprint for enterprise scale, least privilege and bounded
failure.

Implement project factory and lifecycle automation through version-controlled automation and policy checks.

Troubleshoot organization policy and centralized evidence using provider-native telemetry and repeatable
evidence.

Deliver a sanitized portfolio artifact for design and test a google cloud landing-zone hierarchy. Core Concepts
Organization, folders and project hierarchy
Organization, folders and project hierarchy is a design boundary, not merely a console feature. In Google Cloud
Organization, Folders, Projects and Landing Zones, the team must document ownership, trust assumptions,
dependency direction, failure impact and the evidence used to prove the control. The recommended
implementation uses Google Cloud organization, Folders, Projects, Organization Policy Service only where they
satisfy an explicit requirement; equivalent services are not automatically interchangeable. Landing-zone design and enterprise foundation blueprint
A production implementation of Landing-zone design and enterprise foundation blueprint separates the
management plane from workload execution and constrains blast radius.

g-zone design and enterprise foundation blueprint

management plane from workload execution and constrains blast radius. Architecture reviews should evaluate
quotas, regional behavior, identity propagation, private connectivity, encryption, logging and recovery. The
operational contract must state who changes the control, who monitors it and how an emergency exception
expires. Project factory and lifecycle automation
For Project factory and lifecycle automation, repeatability matters more than a one-time successful
deployment. Infrastructure as code, policy tests, deployment verification, drift detection and rollback evidence
should be retained together. A design is incomplete when it works only for the original engineer or depends on
undocumented console steps. Organization policy and centralized evidence

test and a failure test. Teams should prove normal workload behavior, demonstrate that prohibited behavior is
blocked and exercise recovery under a bounded fault. Metrics, logs, audit events and cost records become part
of the acceptance package. Service and Capability Map

Hands-on Lab 31: Design and Test a Google Cloud Landing-Zone Hierarchy
Prerequisites

Disposable provider sandbox or a local simulation.

Terraform or provider CLI, Git and a diagramming tool.


Landing Zones?
Make responsibility and failure boundaries explicit, then automate controls and prove them with normal,
denied and recovery tests rather than trusting a successful deployment alone.
2. How would you choose between the main Google Cloud services in this domain?
Start with workload requirements for latency, state, scale, compliance, team capability, recovery and cost. Select the managed service whose operating model fits those requirements and document the
consequences in an ADR.

Architecture and threat models, reviewed IaC plan, effective-access results, network and encryption tests,
known audit events, SLO and recovery validation, ownership metadata, budget routing and rollback
evidence.

1. What is the most important design principle in Google Cloud Enterprise Foundation Capstone?
Make responsibility and failure boundaries explicit, then automate controls and prove them with normal,
denied and recovery tests rather than trusting a successful deployment alone.
2. How would you choose between the main Google Cloud services in this domain?
Start with workload requirements for latency, state, scale, compliance, team capability, recovery and cost. Select the managed service whose operating model fits those requirements and document the
consequences in an ADR.
3. What evidence would you require before production approval?
Architecture and threat models, reviewed IaC plan, effective-access results, network and encryption tests,
known audit events, SLO and recovery validation, ownership metadata, budget routing and rollback
evidence.
4. How do you reduce provider lock-in without creating a lowest-common-denominator platform?
Preserve portable source, data, interfaces and deployment artifacts where a credible exit scenario requires
them, while still using provider-specific capabilities when their measurable value exceeds migration and
